sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Freyr** (*freyr*) ​— Fertility, ‌Sunshine, Rain · ‌Lord — ​is the Vanir ​god who ​became the Æsir's ​own lord ​of the growing ‌world: son ​of [[njordr|Njǫrðr]], brother ​of [[freyja|Freyja]], ‌ruler of rain ​and sunshine ‌and the fruit ​of the ‌earth, the god ​Snorri says ​it is good ​to call ​on for *ár ​ok frið* ‌— harvest ​and peace.[^1]

Old ‌Norse *Freyr* ​descends from Proto-Germanic ‌*frawjaz* ‘lord’ ​— the same ‌word as ​Gothic *frauja* and ‌Old English ​*frēa* — and ​forms a ‌title-pair with *Freyja* ‌‘lady’. His ‌mythology is the ​corpus's clearest ​economy of sacrifice: ‌the self-wielding ​sword given to ​Skírnir as ‌the price of ​Gerðr's love, ​the improvised antler ‌that killed ​the giant Beli, ‌and the ​fatal absence of ​that sword ​when he faces ​[[surtr|Surtr]] at ‌Ragnarök.[^2] To the ‌Swedes of ​Heimskringla he is ‌also the ​euhemerized King Freyr ​of Uppsala, ‌the peace-years king ‌of the ‌Yngling line.[^3]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as **Freyr** ‌— identical ​to the ASCII ​input, because ​normalized Old Norse ‌writes no ​diacritic in ​this name. The ​mechanical rule ‌therefore places it ​in Tier ​2: nothing distinctive ​is lost ‌in transit, a ​statement about ‌orthography, never about ​the god's ‌standing. The plain-ASCII ​domain freyr.com ‌is registered to ‌a third ​party outside the ​collection and ​is watched for ​release; the ‌project claims no ‌domain for ​this temple.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23–24 (the Vanir; Freyr's rule over rain, sunshine, and the fruit of the earth), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Skírnismál; Lokasenna 42; Vǫluspá 52–53 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 10–13, trans. Alison Finlay and Anthony Faulkes, 2nd ed. (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 2014).

Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Freyr; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Freyr.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in normalized Old ‌Norse as ​**Freyr** (nominative; genitive ​*Freys*). It ​is not a ​personal name ​in the ordinary ‌sense but ​the common noun ​for a ‌master: Proto-Germanic ​*frawjaz* ‘lord’, the ‌ancestor of ​Gothic *frauja* — ‌Ulfilas's word ​for the Lord ​— and ​the Old English ​poetic *frēa* ​‘lord’ of kings ‌and of ​God.[^1] Its feminine ‌counterpart is ​*Freyja* ‘the Lady’, ‌from *frawjōn*; ​the siblings are, ‌etymologically, simply ​‘the Lord’ and ‌‘the Lady’. ​The final *-r* ​is the ‌Old Norse ‌nominative masculine ending.

‌The name ​also travels under ​older bynames. ‌Lokasenna names him ​*Ingunar-Freyr*, and ​Ynglingatal and the ‌Skáldskaparmál tradition ​give *Yngvi-Freyr* — ​the element ‌scholars connect, with ​due caution, ‌to the Ing ​of the ​Old English Rune ​Poem and ​the Inguaeones of ‌Tacitus.[^2]

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **f** ‌→ **F** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **r** ‌→ **r** — ‌Same
- ‌**e** → **e** ‌— Same
​- **y** → ‌**y** — ​Same
- **r** ​→ **r** ​— Same

Because ‌the restoration ​preserves nothing the ​ASCII form ​loses — no ‌diacritic, no ​thorn or eth, ​no length ​mark — the ‌name is ​classified Tier 2 ‌by the ​project's mechanical ‌rule. The plain-ASCII ​domain freyr.com ‌is registered to ‌a third ​party outside the ​collection and ​is watched for ​release; the ‌project claims no ‌domain for ​this temple.

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Freyr (*frawjaz ‘Herr’).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Freyr, Ing.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/ˈfrœy.r̩/** ​— Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **Fr-** — ​Voiceless labiodental ‌[f] and ​trilled [r], ​a common Old ‌Norse onset ​cluster
- ‌**-ey-** — ​The falling diphthong ‌/œy/, born ​by umlaut ​and monophthong-smoothing from ​an older ​*au*; it ​sits between ‌the ‘oy’ of ​English *boy* ‌and the ​‘ay’ of ‌*day*, and survives ​in modern ‌Icelandic as ​/ei/ (Icelanders say ‌‘FRAY-ir’)
- ​**-r** — ​The syllabic ‌trill [r̩] of ‌the nominative ‌masculine ending, ​carrying its ​own light beat

‌For the ​modern speaker, ​the closest approximation ‌is: ‘FRAY-ur’ ​— one ​syllable for ‌the diphthong, then ​the light ‌final trill.

​Kindred and ​historical forms of ​the name:

​- **Proto-Germanic** ‌— *frawjaz*, ‘lord’
‌- **Younger ​Futhark (normalized)** ‌— ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ, ​frauR, the Viking-Age ​carving, keeping ‌the older ‌*au* before ‌it smoothed to ‌ey
- ​**Gothic** — ‌frauja, ‘lord’, the ​Gospels' word ​for the ​Lord
- ‌**Old English** — ​frēa, the ​poetic ‘lord’ ​of Beowulf's ‌kings
- **Modern ​Icelandic** — ​Freyr, the ​name's unbroken living ‌form

Freyr ​is Tier ‌2 because ​the restoration is ‌orthographically complete ​as it ‌stands: normalized ‌Old Norse writes ​this name ​in plain ​ASCII, and there ​is nothing ‌for the ‌ASCII alphabet ​to lose.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Freyr.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval ‌Icelandic manuscripts in ​the Latin ​alphabet as ​**Freyr** — Old ​Norse (North ​Germanic), attested ‌13th c. CE ​in the ​Codex Regius of ‌the Poetic ​Edda and ‌the sister codices ​of the ‌Prose Edda, ​recording material centuries ​older.[^1] Before ​the Latin ​bookhand, Old Norse ​names were ‌carved in ​the younger futhark; ‌no runic ​attestation of ‌this theonym survives, ​so the ‌manuscript form is ​the primary ‌witness, with ​a normalized runic ​rendering standing ‌in for ‌the Viking-Age shape.

‌The scholarly ​rendering proceeds ​step by step:

‌- The ​word is ​the common noun ‌*freyr* ‘lord’, ​from Proto-Germanic ​*frawjaz*, with the ‌nominative singular ​ending *-r*.
- ‌The diphthong ​*ey* descends ​from older *au* ​(still visible ​in a ‌normalized younger-futhark carving, ‌ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ *frauR*); ​the manuscripts' ‌*ey* is the ​smoothed Old ​Icelandic form.
‌- Normalized Old ‌Norse writes ‌the name ‌in plain ASCII ​— no ‌diacritic, no thorn ​or eth ​— so ​the Unicode restoration ‌**Freyr** is ​letter-for-letter the ​manuscript form, capitalized.[^2]
​- Because ‌the name ​is pure ASCII, ​its domain ​was registered ‌decades ago in ​the ordinary ‌way: freyr.com ​is held by ‌a third ​party outside the ‌PuniCodex collection ‌and is ​watched for release; ​no form ​of the ​name is currently ‌owned, and ‌this temple ​claims none.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Freyr; de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Brill, 1962), s.v. Freyr.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Freyr** ​is the ‌god of ‌the peace-years: ​the Vanir ​lord whose ​portfolio Snorri ​fixes in ​a single ‌sentence — ​rain and ​sunshine, the ‌fruit of ​the earth, ‌the prosperity ​of men ‌— and ​whom the ​Swedes remembered ​as the ​king in ​whose days ‌the ​Fróði-peace began.[^1]

‌### Harvest

​‘He rules ‌over rain ​and sunshine, ‌and therewith ​the fruit ‌of the ​earth’; it ​is good ‌to call ‌on him ‌for harvest ​— *ár*. ​The golden-bristled ‌boar and ​the elf-realm ​tooth-gift belong ‌to the ​same shining, ​growing world.[^1]

‌### ​Prosperity

Snorri ‌adds: ‘he ​also governs ​the prosperity ​of men’. ​The euhemerized ‌tradition turns ‌that portfolio ​into economics ‌— King ​Freyr gathers ​the land-rents ‌and the ‌*Uppsala auðr*, ‌the wealth ‌of Uppsala, ​into his ‌own hand, ​and his ​mound swallows ​three years ‌of ​tribute.[^2]

### ​Kingship

Yngvi-Freyr ​stands at ‌the fountainhead ​of the ​Ynglings, the ​dynasty of ‌Uppsala from ​which medieval ‌Norway's and ​Sweden's kings ‌traced their ​lines; his ‌reign is ‌the North's ​canonical portrait ​of sacral ​kingship, the ​king as ‌guarantee of ‌season and ​peace.[^2][^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 24, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 10–13, trans. Finlay and Faulkes (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Freyr.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography ​of Freyr ‌is the ‌richest of ​any Vanir ​god — ​a full ​set of ​attributes fixed by ‌the Eddas ​and the ​cult reports ‌alike:[^1]

- ​**Gullinbursti** — ‌The golden-bristled ​boar forged ‌by Brokkr and ​Sindri, faster ​than any ​horse through ​air and ​water, its ‌bristles lighting ​night to ‌day; Freyr rode ​it — ‌or drove ​behind it ‌— to ​[[baldr|Baldr]]'s pyre
‌- **Skíðblaðnir** ​— The ​best of ships, ‌built by ‌the sons ‌of Ívaldi: ​fair wind ​at every ‌hoisting, room ​for all ​the Æsir armed, ‌and it ​folds like ​cloth into ‌a pouch
​- **The ‌self-wielding sword** ​— The ​blade that fights ​by itself ​for the ‌wise, surrendered ‌to Skírnir ​as the ‌price of ​the errand ​to Gerðr
- ‌**The hart's ‌antler** — ‌The improvised ‌weapon with ​which he ‌killed the ​giant Beli ​bare-handed; the sign ​of the ‌swordless god
​- **Álfheimr** ​— The ​realm of ‌the elves, ​given him ​by the gods ​as a ‌tooth-gift in ​the first ‌days
- ​**The phallus** ‌— The ​cult attribute ‌Adam of Bremen ‌reports at ​Uppsala and ​the Rällinge ​statuette displays: ​fertility written ‌on the ‌body of ​the god[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (the dwarfs' gifts; Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa) and Gylfaginning 24, 37, 44, 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum IV.26–27, trans. Francis J. Tschan (New York: Columbia University Press, 1959).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Freyr's surviving mythology is ​built on a single economy — ‌what the lord of plenty gives away ‌— told across the two Eddas ​and the kings' sagas with unusual coherence.[^1]

​### The Tooth-Gift (Grímnismál 5)

The ​gods gave Álfheimr to Freyr as a ​tooth-gift — the present made to a ​child when its first tooth appears. ‌The detail is the Edda's way of ​saying the elf-realm has always been ​his; Snorri pairs it with the fixed ‌formula of his office: rule over ​rain, sunshine, and the fruit of the ‌earth, and the governing of men's ​prosperity.[^2]

### The Price of Gerðr (Skírnismál)

‌Seated in Hliðskjálf, Óðinn's all-seeing high ​seat, Freyr looked north into Jǫtunheimr and ​saw Gerðr, daughter of the giant Gymir, ​whose white arms lit sky and ​sea as she walked from hall to ​bower. The longing that followed was ‌a sickness: he would not eat, sleep, ​or speak. [[njordr|Njǫrðr]] sent the servant ‌Skírnir to bargain the cause out of ​him, and Skírnir named his price ‌for the wooing-errand — Freyr's horse and ​his sword, the one that fights ‌by itself if he is wise who ​wields it. Freyr paid both on the ‌spot. Skírnir rode through the magic ​flame, broke Gerðr's refusal with gifts, runes, ​and threats, and won her promise ‌to meet Freyr in the grove Barri ‌nine nights hence. The poem closes ‌on the waiting god: ‘Long is one ​night, longer is two — how ​shall I endure three?’[^3]

### The Gifts ‌of the Dwarfs (Skáldskaparmál)

Two of ​the six treasures of the gods are ​Freyr's. Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, was ‌made by the sons of Ívaldi ​— big enough for all the Æsir ​with their war-gear, always granted a ‌fair wind, foldable into a pouch. Gullinbursti, ​the golden-bristled boar, came from the ‌same wager between Loki and the smith ​Brokkr that produced [[thor|Þórr]]'s hammer. Úlfr ​Uggason's Húsdrápa, carved on a hall's panels ​in Iceland about 983 and quoted ​by Snorri, remembers Freyr riding the boar ‌to Baldr's funeral; Gylfaginning gives him a ‌chariot drawn by Gullinbursti for the ​same journey.[^4]

### Swordless Against Surtr (Vǫluspá ‌52–53; Gylfaginning 51)

The Edda keeps ​the ledger. In Lokasenna, [[tyr|Týr]] throws the ​old bargain in Freyr's face: with ‌gold you bought Gymir's daughter and sold ‌your sword — when Muspell's sons ‌ride through the dark wood you will ‌not know what to fight with. ​Gylfaginning recalls that Freyr once killed the ‌giant Beli with a hart's antler and ​could have slain him with his ​fist; but at Ragnarök improvisation ends. Freyr ​goes against [[surtr|Surtr]], and his death, ‌Snorri says, comes the harder because he ​lacks the good sword he gave ​Skírnir. Vǫluspá's seeress watches the shining lord ​fall before the fire.[^5]

### The ‌King Who Would Not Die (Ynglinga saga ​10–13)

Heimskringla's euhemerized Freyr is king ​of the Swedes at Uppsala after Njǫrðr: ​he built the great temple, gathered the ‌land-rents and the wealth of Uppsala ​into his own hand, and in his ‌days began the Fróði-peace, the peace-years ​of good seasons the Swedes credited to ‌their king. When he died, his ​men concealed it: they set him in ‌a mound with three holes, told ‌the people he lived, and for three ​years the tribute — gold, silver, ​copper — was poured down into the ​mound while the peace held. Afterwards the ​Swedes still would not burn him; ‌they called him the god of the ‌world and sacrificed to him for ​peace and good seasons.[^6]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Freyr.
Grímnismál 5; Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 24, trans. Larrington (2014) and Faulkes (1987).
Skírnismál (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (the dwarfs' gifts; Húsdrápa) and Gylfaginning 44, 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lokasenna 42; Vǫluspá 52–53 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 37, 51, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 10–13, trans. Finlay and Faulkes (2014).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Freyr's name ​is a ‌title, and ‌titles travel farther ​than theonyms. ​His Proto-Germanic ​*frawjaz* ‘lord’ is ​Gothic *frauja* ​— the word ‌Ulfilas's Bible ​uses for ​the Lord — ‌and the ​Old English ‌poetic *frēa*, the ​‘lord’ of ‌Beowulf's kings; ​his sister [[freyja|Freyja]] ​is the ​same word in ​the feminine.[^1]

​The older ‌debate runs through ​his bynames. ‌Lokasenna calls ​him *Ingunar-Freyr*; Ynglingatal ‌and Snorri ​derive the ‌Yngling dynasty from ​*Yngvi-Freyr*. Since ‌Grimm, scholars have ​connected that ​Ing-element with ‌the Inguaeones of ‌Tacitus's Germania ‌2 — ​the peoples descended ​from Mannus ‌through Ing ​— and with ​the Ing ‌of the Old ​English Rune ​Poem, ‘first ‌among the East ​Danes seen ‌by men’ ​before he went ​east over ​the wave. ​The equation Ing ‌= Yngvi ‌= Freyr is ​argued, not ‌proven; Simek ​counsels caution, and ​the manuscripts ‌do not ‌settle it.[^2] What ‌the outside ‌world saw ​plainly is recorded ‌by Adam ​of Bremen: at ​Uppsala the ​Swedes called ‌the god *Fricco*, ​granted him ​*pacem voluptatemque* ​— peace and ‌pleasure — ​and set ​him ithyphallic between ​Thor and ‌Wodan, a Germanic ​Priapus inside ‌a triad ​of his own.[^3] ‌Within the ​corpus his ‌closest kin are ‌[[njordr|Njǫrðr]] his ​father and ​[[freyja|Freyja]] his twin ​in title ​— the Vanir ‌triad of ‌wealth, sea, ​and season.

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Freyr, Freyja.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Freyr, Ing, Inguaeones; Tacitus, Germania 2.
Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum IV.26–27, trans. Tschan (1959).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Freyr ​never left ‌the North. ‌His cult ​geography ​survives on ​the map ​in hundreds ​of ‌theophoric place-names ​— Frøysland, ​Frøsvoll, Frösåker, ‌Fröslunda and ​their ‌kin across ​Norway and ‌Sweden — ​the ​densest fertility-god ​landscape in ​Scandinavian onomastics, ​many ‌compounded with ​‘grove’, ‘field’, ‌and ‘meadow’.[^1] ​The ‌name itself ​lives on ‌as a ​Scandinavian ‌given name: ​Freyr in ​Iceland, Frej ‌in Denmark ‌and ‌Sweden.

His ​historical afterlife ​is the ‌Yngling ​one: medieval ​Norwegian and ‌Swedish royal ​genealogies ​traced their ‌lines through ​the Ynglings ‌of ​Uppsala to ​Yngvi-Freyr, making ​the peace-years ​king ‌the dynastic ‌ancestor of ​two kingdoms, ‌and ​Snorri's portrait ​became the ‌North's standing ‌image of ‌the ‌good reign ​— the ‌king whose ​death ​the realm ​refused to ‌admit.[^2] Modern ​Heathen ​and Ásatrú ​communities keep ‌him at ​the ​centre of ​harvest and ‌fertility blóts ​under ‌the old ​formula *ár ‌ok frið*, ​and the ‌golden ‌boar runs ​through modern ​jewellery, fantasy, ​and ​games as ‌the sun-animal ‌of the ​Vanir.[^3]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Freyr (cult and place-names).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 10–13; Þjóðólfr of Hvin, Ynglingatal, trans. Finlay and Faulkes (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Freyr.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Freyr is ​one of ‌the few ‌Norse gods ​with a ​plausible cult-image in ​the ground. ​The Rällinge ​statuette — ‌a small ​seated bronze of ​the Viking ‌Age, found ​in 1904 ‌at Rällinge, ​Lunda parish, Södermanland, ‌Sweden — ​shows a ​cross-legged, bearded, ​unmistakably ithyphallic ​figure and has ​been identified ‌as Freyr ​since its ‌discovery; it matches ​Adam of ‌Bremen's description ​of the ‌Uppsala *Fricco* ​with striking economy.[^1]

‌Uppsala itself ​anchors the ​cult landscape: ‌Adam describes ‌the great temple, ‌its golden ​chain, and ​its triad ‌of Thor, ​Wodan, and Fricco ​around 1075, ‌and the ​royal mounds ​of Gamla ‌Uppsala still stand ​where Ynglinga ‌saga sets ​King Freyr's ​own mound ​and the *Uppsala ​auðr*.[^2] The ‌theophoric place-name ‌record — ​hundreds of ‌Frøy-/Frö- names, weighted ​to groves ​and fields ‌— is ‌the strongest ‌indirect witness of ‌a working ​fertility cult.[^3] ‌Against all ​this, the ​runic corpus is ​silent: no ‌surviving inscription ​invokes the ​god by name. ​The literary ‌witnesses are ​the Codex ​Regius poems ​(Skírnismál, Grímnismál, Lokasenna, ‌Vǫluspá) and ​the quotation ‌of Úlfr ​Uggason's Húsdrápa ‌(c. 983) in ​Skáldskaparmál, which ‌proves the ‌boar-riding Freyr ​was already ​a fixture of ​pre-Christian hall ​decoration a ‌generation before ‌the conversion ​of Iceland.[^4]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Freyr (Rällinge statuette).
Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum IV.26–27, trans. Tschan (1959); Snorri Sturluson, Ynglinga saga 10–13.
de Vries, Jan, Altgermanische Religionsgeschichte, 2nd ed., 2 vols. (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1956–57), on the Freyr cult and place-names.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (Húsdrápa quotation), trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.body:
The account ​of Freyr given in ‌this edition rests on ‌the witnesses and ​reference works listed below. ​The Poetic Edda supplies ​the mythic narrative; ​the Prose Edda and ​Heimskringla the systematic and ‌euhemerized portraits; Adam ​of Bremen the outside ​report on the living ‌cult; the lexica and ​handbooks secure the ‌name's etymology and the ​scholarly debates.

- [^1] ‌The Poetic Edda, ​trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ​ed. (Oxford: Oxford University ​Press, 2014): Skírnismál ​(the wooing of Gerðr); ​Grímnismál 5 (Álfheimr); Lokasenna ‌42–43 (the sword ​sold; Ingunar-Freyr); Vǫluspá 52–53 ‌(Freyr against Surtr); Vafþrúðnismál ​38–39 (the Vanir ‌hostage).
- [^2] Snorri ​Sturluson, Edda, ed. and ‌trans. Anthony Faulkes ​(London: Everyman, 1987): Gylfaginning ‌23–24, 37, 44, 49, ​51; Skáldskaparmál (the ​dwarfs' gifts; Úlfr Uggason's ‌Húsdrápa).
- [^3] Snorri ‌Sturluson, Heimskringla: Ynglinga saga ‌10–13; Þjóðólfr of ​Hvin, Ynglingatal, trans. Alison ​Finlay and Anthony Faulkes, ‌2nd ed. (London: ​Viking Society for Northern ​Research, 2014).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The ​Poetic Edda ‌gives Freyr ‌one whole ​poem and ​a string ​of load-bearing ​stanzas. *Skírnismál* ​— the ‌poem the ​Codex Regius ​titles *För ‌Skírnis*, ‘Skírnir's ​journey’ ‌— is ​his full ‌narrative: the ​forbidden seat ​in Hliðskjálf, ​the sight ​of Gerðr ​lighting sky ‌and sea, ​the lovesickness, ‌the bargain ​of ‌horse and ​sword, Skírnir's ‌ride through ​the magic ‌flame, the ​wooing won ​by gifts ‌and threats, ‌and the ‌nine-night wait ​to Barri.[^1]

​Around it ‌the ​other poems ​keep his ‌accounts. *Grímnismál* ​5 records ​the tooth-gift ‌of Álfheimr. ​*Lokasenna* 42–43 ‌holds the ​tradition's sharpest ​summary — ​Týr's taunt ​that ‌Freyr bought ‌Gymir's daughter ​with gold ‌and sold ​his sword ​— and ‌preserves his ‌byname Ingunar-Freyr.[^2] ‌*Vǫluspá* 52–53 ‌stages the ​reckoning: when ‌Surtr comes ​from ​the south ​with the ‌bane of ​branches, Freyr ​goes against ​him and ‌falls, the ​shining lord ​against the ​fire. *Vafþrúðnismál* ‌38–39 supplies ​the ‌frame: Njǫrðr ​was made ‌among the ​Vanir and ‌given to ‌the Æsir ​as a ​hostage — ​the exchange ​by which ‌the peace-gods ‌came to ​Ásgarðr.[^3]

sources.citation: Skírnismál (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose ​Edda is ‌Freyr's systematic ‌witness. Gylfaginning 23–24 ​sets his ​place in the ​pantheon — ​the Vanir ​hostages Njǫrðr and ‌Freyr accepted ​among the Æsir ​— and ‌fixes the ​office in the ‌tradition's most ​quoted sentence: ‌Freyr rules rain ​and sunshine ​and the fruit ​of the ​earth, is ​good to call ‌on for ​harvest and peace, ‌and governs ​the prosperity ‌of men; Álfheimr ​was his ‌tooth-gift.[^1]

Gylfaginning then ​keeps returning ‌to him ​at the hinge-points ​of the ‌mythology: 37 ‌remembers that he ‌killed the ​giant Beli with ​a hart's ‌antler and ​could have slain ​him with ‌his fist; 44 ​ranks Skíðblaðnir ​among the ‌chief things of ​the world, ‌the best ​of ships, made ​by the ​sons of Ívaldi ​and foldable ‌into a ‌pouch; 49 brings ​him to ‌Baldr's pyre in ​a chariot ​drawn by ‌Gullinbursti; and 51 ‌closes the ‌account — ‌at Ragnarök Freyr ​fights Surtr, ‌and falls the ​harder for ​lacking the ​good sword he ‌gave Skírnir.[^2] ​Skáldskaparmál supplies the ​making of ​the treasures ‌— the sons ​of Ívaldi's ​ship, Brokkr and ​Sindri's boar ‌from the ​same wager that ‌forged Mjǫllnir ​— and ‌quotes Úlfr Uggason's ​Húsdrápa, carved ‌hall-panels of c. ‌983 showing ​Freyr riding ​the boar to ​Baldr's funeral: ​proof the myth ‌was a ‌fixture of ​pre-Christian art.[^3]

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no ​invocation of ​Freyr: ​no runestone ​asks ​his ‌favour, no ​amulet ​bears his ‌name, ​and no ‌inscription ​yet ‌found links ​a ​dedicant to ​his ​cult ​— a ‌striking ​silence for ‌a ​god ‌whose place-names ​carpet ‌two kingdoms, ​and ‌a ​reminder that ​runic ‌stones are ‌monuments ‌of families, ​not ​temple ‌books.[^1]

What ​the ​younger futhark ‌can ​show ​is the ‌name's ​older shape. ‌A ​normalized ​Viking-Age carving ​would ​read **ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ**, ‌*frauR*: ‌the ​ᚢ-rune writing ‌the ​*au* that ​had ‌not yet ‌smoothed ‌to ‌*ey* everywhere, ​and ‌ᛦ — ​the ​yr-rune ​— writing ‌the ​final nominative ​*-r*. ​The ‌runic form ​sits ​visibly closer ​to ‌Proto-Germanic ​*frawjaz* ‘lord’ ‌than ​the manuscript ‌spelling ​does: in ‌runes, ‌the ​Lord's name ​still ​remembers the ​two-syllable ‌word ‌it grew ​from.[^2]

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
The saga ​corpus preserves ‌Freyr's living cult ‌from both ​sides of the ​conversion. Heimskringla's ​*Ynglinga saga* euhemerizes ​him as the ​peace-years king ‌of Uppsala — ​builder of ​the temple, holder ‌of the ​*Uppsala auðr*, the ‌king whose ​concealed death held ‌the Fróði-peace ​for three years ​while the tribute ​poured into ​his mound — ​and *Hákonar ‌saga góða* shows ​the heathen ‌sacrifice still demanding ​kingship's compliance ‌generations later.[^1]

Icelandic ​family sagas ‌keep the cult ​personal. *Hrafnkels saga ‌Freysgoða* is ​built on a ​Freyr-priest's devotion: ‌Hrafnkell, goði of ‌Freyr, shares ‌his best possessions ​with the ​god and dedicates ‌the stallion ​Freyfaxi to him, ​with a vow ‌to kill ​any man who ​rides it ‌— the vow ​the whole ‌saga springs. *Vatnsdœla ​saga* remembers ​Ingimundr's little silver ​Freyr amulet, ​lost and found ‌at the spot ‌where he ​settles in Iceland ‌— the ​god choosing his ​own homestead.[^2] ‌The mission-age þættir ‌strike back ‌with comedy: *Ǫgmundar ‌þáttr dytts* ​has a Swedish ‌Freyr idol hauled ​around the ​country for offerings, ​while *Gunnars ‌þáttr helmings* turns ​the same ​procession into a ​tale of ‌a Norwegian exile ​impersonating the ​god.[^3] And from ​the outside, Adam ‌of Bremen's ​account of the ‌Uppsala temple ​(c. 1075) — ‌Fricco ithyphallic ​between Thor and ‌Wodan, granter ‌of peace and ​pleasure, honoured ​at weddings — ​remains the single ​most vivid ‌report of the ‌god's cult ​ever written.[^4]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Freyr ​is the ‌god who ‌teaches ​what lordship ​costs. His ​name ​is not ​a name ‌at ​all but ​the word ‌‘Lord’ ​itself — ‌every king ​and ‌every master ​borrowing his ​title ​for as ​long as ​the ‌peace holds. ​And the ‌peace ​holds only ‌by giving: ​the ‌sword for ​the bride, ‌the ​tribute for ​the mound, ‌the ‌life for ‌the world ​at ​Ragnarök.[^1]

The ‌Edda's arithmetic ​is ​merciless — ‌the self-wielding ​sword ​is the ‌one thing ​that cannot ‌be ​given away ​and kept ​— ​but Freyr ‌gives it ‌anyway, ​for love, ‌in a ​single ​scene, without ‌a regret ‌the ‌poems record. ‌The tradition ​honours ‌him not ​for the ​fight ​he loses ‌but for ​the ​peace-years he ​bought while ‌he ​could: rain ​and sunshine ​in ‌their season, ​the fruit ‌of ​the earth, ‌the prosperity ​of ‌men. The ‌lord of ​plenty ​is the ​god of ​the ‌gift you ‌cannot take ​back.

sources.citation: Skírnismál; Vǫluspá 52–53 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
